place: A riverside clearing after a night of rain; the ground and gathered branches are still damp.
things: dry tinder found under a log
outcome: The damp branches will not catch from sparks alone; the flint throws sparks onto wet bark that just smokes. Once the player digs out dry tinder from under a fallen log and shields it from the breeze, the sparks catch and a small flame builds, which then dries and lights the damp branches stacked over it. Getting a proper fire going takes several tries and some minutes longer than it would with dry wood.

numbers: how many strikes before a spark catches
how much moisture is in the wood

effects: player learns where dry tinder is
numbers: how long the search takes
how many strikes it takes
how long until the branches catch
how much heat is needed to dry them first

latent: dry tinder under the fallen log
stress: fuel readiness (moisture) gates whether ignition succeeds, and drying is itself a precondition before burning can start
temptation: a special rule that damp branches specifically need tinder-then-branches, instead of a general moisture property that resists ignition until heat and time reduce it

place: A dry hillside pasture in late summer, grass knee-high and brittle, a hedge and a neighbor's haystack downwind at the bottom of the slope.
lines: set the whole field on fire
put it out, put it out
outcome: The grass is dry and catches at once, and the wind carries the flame line downhill faster than the player can contain it. Beating at the edge with a cloak slows it in places but does not stop it; by the time it reaches the bottom of the slope it has caught the hedge and singed the corner of the haystack before neighbors arrive to help smother it. What was meant as a small controlled burn becomes a hillside fire that takes most of an afternoon to put out and leaves a wide blackened scar.

numbers: how fast the flame line spreads

effects: observer learns the fire is spreading
numbers: how far it travels before help arrives
how much the wind speeds it
how much of the hedge burns
how long it takes several people to put out

latent: how far downhill the haystack sits from the ignition point
stress: scale and spread rate from a single ignition, and containment failing to keep pace with propagation
temptation: a rule that treats 'field' as one object that either burns or doesn't, instead of grass-by-patch spread driven by a wind property and a slope property

place: A hearth in a stone hut after a rainy day's walk; boots are soaked through.
lines: dry my boots by the fire
outcome: Set at a sensible distance the boots would simply dry over an hour or so, but pulled in close for a faster result they sit near enough that the leather grows hot rather than just warm. Left unwatched while the player does something else, the boots stiffen and the leather at the toe scorches and cracks before anyone notices the smell; they are still wearable but never sit right again.

numbers: how long it takes to dry at a safe distance

because: patient is close to the fire
numbers: how close counts as too close
how long before scorching starts
how long unattended before damage sets in

state_after: boots: dry, scorched at the toe, stiff
stress: distance from heat as a continuous property, where drying and scorching sit on the same curve rather than being different rules
temptation: a specific 'boots near fire' rule instead of a general heat-and-distance-over-time function that applies to any object near a flame

place: A smithy with a coal forge, a hammer and anvil, and a trough of water.
lines: heat the blade till it glows
outcome: The blade heats to a dull red and then bright orange under the bellows; worked at the right heat the bend hammers out cleanly. Quenched quickly in the water it hisses and hardens at once. Rushed and left in the fire a little too long, though, the metal has actually overheated past where hammering helps; the blade looks fine leaving the forge, but days later, put to hard use, it cracks along the overheated section rather than bending.

numbers: how long to reach working heat
how hot is too hot
how many strikes to straighten it
how fast it cools
how brittle it becomes if it was overheated first
how many days pass before it is struck hard enough to fail

latent: whether the blade was heated past the safe working point, invisible until it fails
state_after: iron blade: hardened, straight, latently brittle, later cracked
stress: a hidden state (overheated) that does not show until a delayed, unrelated event reveals it
temptation: checking only the final quench temperature instead of tracking how long the metal sat at excessive heat beforehand

place: A trapper's camp at dusk, a low fire banked with coals, a cooking pot set near the edge, and a fresh pelt hung to dry on a rack just above.
outcome: Drawn by the smell of grease in the pot, the fox noses it over; it tips into the coals and spills fat that flares up briefly, and the flare licks up into the pelt hanging just above on the rack. The pelt is fur, and fur close to open flame catches fast: a patch of it singes and curls before the trapper returns to beat it out, leaving a ruined section of the hide.

numbers: how much fat spills
how high the flare reaches
how long it lasts

because: patient is close above the fire
numbers: how much of the pelt burns before it is beaten out

stress: a creature's ordinary behavior (foraging) triggering a fire hazard with nobody present to intend it
temptation: a scripted 'fox steals food' event instead of deriving the knock from hunger plus an unstable, food-smelling object in reach

place: The same smithy, later, with a puddle of lamp oil spilled near the anvil from an earlier refill.
outcome: A stray spark thrown off the anvil lands in the puddle of oil nobody noticed on the floor. Oil catches far more readily than the packed dirt around it and flashes up suddenly around the smith's feet; singed eyebrows and a scorched boot cuff are the result before it is stamped out. Nothing else catches, since the floor itself will not burn, but the fright costs the smith the rest of the afternoon's work.

numbers: how far a spark can fly
how much oil is pooled
how quickly it catches
how severe the burn is

latent: the oil puddle nobody had cleaned up
stress: an unnoticed hazard, a thin flammable film, that ordinary sparks harmless on bare dirt ignite instantly
temptation: hardcoding 'oil is dangerous near forges' instead of letting any spark-generating process meet any flammable puddle through their shared properties

place: A campsite in a forest after days of rain; the only wood in reach is a freshly cut green branch and some sodden deadfall.
outcome: Neither piece of wood will take a flame. The green branch is full of sap and living moisture that no amount of sparking will burn off quickly, and the deadfall is soaked through from days of rain; both smoke and hiss without ever catching. Without dry tinder or kindling from somewhere else, the fire simply does not happen, no matter how many times the player tries.

numbers: how many attempts before giving up

because: patient is too wet to ignite
numbers: how wet is too wet to catch

state_after: green branch: unlit, smoking slightly, unchanged
stress: a hard failure case where no property present supports ignition, and the engine must say no rather than fudge a partial success
temptation: letting persistence alone eventually light any wood, instead of moisture and sap content being real gates that effort cannot overcome without a different resource

place: A small cooking fire beside a tent, about to be abandoned for the night.
lines: just dump the water on it
outcome: Dumped straight on, the water does put the fire out, but the sudden contact between water and hot coals throws up a burst of steam right where the player's hand still holds the skin close over the flames. The fire is out and safe to leave, but the player comes away with a light scald across the knuckles that stings for the rest of the evening.

numbers: how much water is needed to fully douse it

because: patient is close to the coals
numbers: how close counts as too close

stress: extinguishing a fire is not a clean, riskless action; the steam it produces carries its own heat that a nearby hand can suffer from
temptation: treating 'douse with water' as a single safe undo of burning, instead of generating a real steam byproduct that can itself burn

place: A hearth in a hut, banked with ash for the night beside a stack of firewood and a wicker basket left too close.
outcome: Banked under ash the coals keep a low heat through most of the night rather than going fully cold, as banked fires do. Toward morning a draft through a gap in the wall stirs the ash aside and feeds the embers enough air that they catch again on their own, and a stray coal rolls against the wicker basket set too close. By the time anyone wakes, the basket has caught and burned down to a blackened ring, though the fire has not spread past it.

numbers: how many hours the coals stay warm under ash

because: place has a gap in the wall

how long the basket takes to burn down

latent: that the coals never fully went out under the ash
state_after: wicker basket: burned to a ring of ash
stress: unobserved time overnight where a banked fire's slow heat loss, not a fixed off-state, decides whether embers are still alive by morning
temptation: modeling 'banked fire' as simply off until morning, instead of a heat value that decays slowly and can still cross the ignition threshold given air

place: A small stone shelter with one low doorway and no chimney, used to wait out a storm.
lines: build a fire in here to warm up
outcome: The fire itself lights fine on the dry kindling brought in, but with no chimney and only a low doorway, the smoke it makes has nowhere to go. It fills the shelter from the ceiling down, and within a few minutes the player is coughing and eyes stinging; staying inside gets worse, not better, the longer the fire burns. Moving the fire to just outside the doorway, or opening it wider, is the only way to get warmth without the smoke.

numbers: how much smoke is made per minute of burning

because: place has a low narrow doorway
numbers: how long before the air is bad
how large the doorway would need to be to vent it
how much smoke exposure becomes dangerous

stress: enclosed space plus no vent turns an otherwise ordinary fire into a hazard purely from geometry, not from the fire itself misbehaving
temptation: a rule specific to 'shelters' having smoke problems instead of a general venting-and-enclosure property that any confined flame-bearing space shares

place: A drying line strung between two trees outside a hut, hung with washed clothes, under a sky that had looked clear that morning.
outcome: The clear morning gives no warning; a rain cloud moves in from the hills within the hour and starts a steady shower. Everything on the line is soaked through again within minutes, undoing the morning's drying, and left long enough the wet cloth starts to smell musty rather than merely being wet, since nobody is there to bring it in.

temptation: a fixed 'it rains sometimes' random event instead of weather that actually wets specific exposed things with a duration and a follow-on state

place: A narrow mountain pass at night, a footpath running close to a drop on one side, lit only by a hand lantern.
outcome: A gust funnels through the pass and snuffs the lantern's flame outright; a small flame in open wind has nothing to shield it. The path is no longer visible, and without light the player has to feel along the rock wall and go slowly rather than risk the drop; relighting is not possible until reaching a place out of the wind, which costs a good deal of time.

temptation: a scripted 'wind sometimes extinguishes lights' chance roll instead of deriving it from flame size versus wind strength, which would also apply to campfires and torches

place: A stone hut's doorstep in early winter, a clay water jug left full and uncovered overnight.
outcome: The temperature drops well below freezing overnight and the water in the jug freezes solid. Water expands as it turns to ice, and the clay has nowhere to give; a crack runs up the side of the jug by morning, and once the ice inside thaws through the day the water leaks straight out of it. The jug is still usable for dry storage but can no longer hold water.

temptation: a rule that says 'jugs left out in winter break' instead of deriving it from freezing expanding a fixed volume of liquid inside a rigid, sealed container

outcome: Snow builds up over several days until it lies deep across the whole area, burying the branch cover and any trace of the pit under a smooth, featureless drift indistinguishable from the ground around it. The vegetables are fine underneath, kept cold, but the cache cannot be found again without either remembering exactly where it was relative to a landmark or waiting for the snow to melt away in spring.

place: A river bend where the current runs slow, ice sheeting over from bank to bank after a cold snap, but only a few days old.
outcome: The ice looks solid but is only a few days old and thinner near the middle where the current runs faster underneath. Partway across it gives way with a crack, dropping the player through into knee-to-waist-deep freezing water. Climbing out onto firmer ice at the edge is possible, but the player is now soaked in near-freezing water some distance from any fire, which is the more dangerous problem.

outcome: The crossing itself is easy and shallow, but it soaks the player's clothes to the waist. Walking on without stopping to dry off, the wet cloth keeps drawing heat away in the cool air far faster than dry clothes would; by the time camp is made hours later the player is properly chilled, shivering, and slower to warm back up even once a fire is finally lit.

place: An open hillside campsite, a lean-to hastily built from branches and broad leaves against an incoming storm.
lines: build a shelter quick, storm's coming
outcome: Built in a hurry with whatever was at hand, the leaf covering is thin and gappy rather than properly layered. It sheds the first light rain well enough, but once the storm's heavier rain and wind arrive, water finds the gaps and drips through steadily, and a gust peels back one loose corner entirely. The player stays drier than out in the open but not properly dry, and spends part of the night re-pinning the corner down.

place: A lone oak on a hilltop pasture during a passing thunderstorm, dry grass around its base after a rainless week.
outcome: Being the tallest thing for some distance, the oak draws the strike. The bolt splits a long strip of bark and wood down one side of the trunk and leaves the exposed wood there smoking, sap boiling out at the split. Whether it becomes more than a scorched tree depends on what is around it: the grass at the base is dry from a rainless week and close enough to the smoking wood that it is only luck, and the rain that follows a few minutes later, that keeps it from catching properly and spreading.

There is technically still water to be had, but it comes up thick with silt and mud rather than clear, and needs settling or straining before it is fit to drink; filling the waterskin the normal way just stirs the bottom and makes it worse.

place: A ploughed field on the way to the quarry, after two days of steady rain.
lines: cut across the field to the quarry
outcome: Two days of rain has turned the loose ploughed soil into deep, sucking mud rather than the firmer ground of the path around the edge. Every step sinks well past the ankle, and partway across, pulling a foot free leaves a boot planted in the mud behind; digging it back out costs time and leaves both boots caked and heavier than before, and the shortcut ends up slower than the longer dry path would have been.
